'''''Spathiphyllum''''' is a genus of 59 species of [[monocotyledon]]ous [[flowering plant]]s in the family [[Araceae]], native to tropical regions of the [[Americas]] and southeastern [[Asia]]. Certain species of ''Spathiphyllum'' are commonly known as '''spath''' or '''peace lilies'''.

They are [[evergreen]] [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]]s with large leaves {{convert|12|–|65|cm}} long and {{convert|3|–|25|cm}} broad. The [[flower]]s are produced in a [[spadix (botany)|spadix]], surrounded by a {{convert|10|–|30|cm}} long, white, yellowish, or greenish [[spathe]]. The plant does not require large amounts of light or water to survive. It is most often grown as a houseplant. However, it can withstand the elements well enough to thrive when planted outdoors in hot and humid environments.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-12-23 |title=Is a peace lily an indoor or outdoor plant? - Gardening Host |url=https://gardeninghost.com/is-a-peace-lily-an-indoor-or-outdoor-plant/ |access-date=2022-12-23 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Spathiphyllum'' is a genus of [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] evergreen plants with dark green foliage that can reach {{convert|1|to|6|ft|m}} in height.<ref name=NCS>{{cite web|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/spathiphyllum/ |accessdate=30 March 2024 |title=Spathiphyllum |publisher=NC State Extension}}</ref> Rosettes of glossy, dark green leaves emerge directly from a low-lying or underground creeping stem.<ref name=Chen2018/><ref name=NCS/> The leaves are elliptical or [[Glossary of leaf morphology|lanceolate]], {{convert|4|to|25|in|cm}} long and {{convert|1|to|10|in|cm}} wide.<ref name=Chen2018>{{cite web|url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/EP161 |accessdate=30 March 2024 |title=Cultural Guidelines for Commercial Production of Interiorscape ''Spathiphyllum'' |vauthors=Chen J, McConnell DB, Henny RJ, Everitt KC |publisher=University of Florida IFAS Extension |date=5 July 2018}}</ref><ref name=NCS/> They are supported on shoots ([[petiole (botany)|petioles]]) of shorter or similar length to the leaf.<ref name=NCS/>

The [[inflorescence|flowering structure]] rises above the foliage, with a single white or greenish-white [[spathe]] (a specialized leaf associated with the flower) partially surrounding the flower structure.<ref name=NCS/> The spathe is elliptical or lanceolate, and {{convert|4|to|12|in|cm}} long.<ref name=NCS/> It surrounds the [[Spadix (botany)|spadix]] (a short fleshy structure that contains the male and female flower parts), which is greenish-white or cream in color, and shorter than the surrounding spathe.<ref name=NCS/> The spadix is covered in equal-sized flowers that contain both the male and female reproductive parts.<ref name=Henny2020>{{cite web|url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/EP366 |accessdate=30 March 2024 |title=Tropical Foliage Plant Development: Breeding Techniques for Anthurium and Spathiphyllum |publisher=University of Florida IFAS Extension |vauthors=Henny RJ, Chen J, Mellich A |date=15 October 2020}}</ref> All ''Spathiphyllum'' flowers on a given spadix mature at the same time, and produce [[pollen]] for up to four days.<ref name=Henny2020/> Pollinated flowers produce ovoid fruits that mature over four to six months, each containing up to eight seeds.<ref name=Henny2020/><ref name=Kew-Desc/>

== Ecology and distribution ==
Members of ''Spathiphyllum'' are widespread in Central America and northern South America. Two species are found on Pacific islands: one on [[Cocos Island]] (''S. laeve'') and one in Indonesia and the Philippines (''S. commutatum''). They grow on the forest floors of tropical humid forests, in shady, moist or wet areas along rivers and streams, in [[river valley]]s and [[foothills]].<ref name=Kew-Desc>{{cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30003632-2/general-information |accessdate=4 April 2024 |title=''Spathiphyllum'' - Descriptions |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew – Plants of the World Online |date= 2011}}</ref><ref name=Bunting1960>{{cite journal|title=A Revision of Spathiphyllum (Araceae) |author=Bunting GS |journal=Memoirs of the New York Botanical Garden |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=1–53 |date=Nov 1960 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/324551 |accessdate=4 April 2024}}</ref> They often grow in colonies along waterways, and can be in places periodically inundated with water.<ref name=Bunting1960/>

== Taxonomy ==

''Spathiphyllum'' includes 59 accepted species.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30003632-2 |accessdate=4 April 2024 |title=Spathiphyllum, Schott |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew – Plants of the World Online}}</ref> Several [[Section (botany)|sections]] of the genus have also been recognized. ''Massowia'', which includes the widespread American ''S. cannifolium'' and the Pacific ''S. laeve'' and ''S. commutatum''; ''Dysspathiphyllum'' containing only the Colombian ''S. humboldtii''; and the larger sections ''Spathiphyllum'' and ''Amomophyllum''.<ref name=Bunting1960/>

== Cultivation and uses ==
[[File:Tab 1 & 2 Vol 3 Annales Musei Botanici Lugduno-Batavi.jpg|thumb|''Spathiphyllum commutatum'' illustration showing dark foliage and contrasting white flowers.]]
''Spathiphyllum'' are popular [[houseplant]]s due to their attractive dark foliage and contrasting white flowers, easy care, and variety of [[cultivar]]s available of different sizes.<ref name=Chen2018/> Commercially, ''Spathiphyllum'' plants are typically propagated by [[plant tissue culture]], then potted up to multi-well plastic trays, then on into larger containers containing [[peat]], [[pine bark]], [[vermiculite]], and/or [[coir]].<ref name=Chen2018/> Plants grow best between {{convert|70|and|90|F|C}}. Once at a size ready for sale, plants are sprayed with [[gibberellic acid]], which induces flowering 9 to 12 weeks after a single treatment.<ref name=Chen2018/>

It lives best in shade and needs little sunlight to thrive, and is watered approximately once a week. The soil is best left moist but only needs watering if the soil is dry.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/02/13/nyregion/cuttings-need-an-air-freshener-try-plants.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm |title=Need an Air Freshener? Try Plants |author=Anne Raver |date=February 13, 1994 |work=New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Wolverton |first1=B.C. |title=Eco-Friendly Houseplants |date=1996 |publisher=George Weidenfeld & Nicolson |isbn=978-0-14-026243-8 |pages=23–25, 32–33, 58–59}}</ref>

The [[cultivar]] 'Mauna Loa' has won the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/78666/Spathiphyllum-Mauna-Loa/Details | title = ''Spathiphyllum'' 'Mauna Loa' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref>

At least one ''Spathiphyllum'' is used as food. The young spadix of ''S. matudae'' is pickled in vinegar, or cooked with eggs.<ref name=Bunting1960/>

== Toxicity ==
Although it is called a "lily", the peace lily is not a true lily from the family [[Liliaceae]]. True lilies are highly toxic (poisonous) to cats and dogs,<ref name="Fitzgerald2010">{{cite journal|last1=Fitzgerald|first1=Kevin T.|title=Lily toxicity in the cat|journal=Topics in Companion Animal Medicine|volume=25|issue=4|year=2010|pages=213–217 |doi=10.1053/j.tcam.2010.09.006|pmid=21147474}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.south-florida-plant-guide.com/peace-lily.html | title=Peace Lily | access-date=1 August 2016}}</ref> but the peace lily, ''Spathiphyllum'' is only mildly toxic to humans and other animals when ingested.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.plantsciences.ucdavis.edu/ce/king/PoisPlant/Tox-COM.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100131132210/http://www.plantsciences.ucdavis.edu/ce/king/PoisPlant/Tox-COM.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=2010-01-31 |title=University of California - Toxic Plants ''(list)'' |access-date=2018-07-12}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.entirelypets.com/toxicplants.html|title=23 Common Flowers That Are Poisonous For Your Pet|website=www.entirelypets.com}}</ref> Like many Araceae, it contains [[calcium oxalate]] crystals, which can cause skin irritation, a burning sensation in the mouth, difficulty swallowing, and nausea,<ref name="aspca">{{cite web | url=http://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/toxic-and-non-toxic-plants/peace-lily | title=Toxic and Non-Toxic Plants - Peace Lily | access-date=1 August 2016}}</ref> but it does not contain the toxins found in true lilies, which can cause acute kidney failure in cats and some other animals.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.petpoisonhelpline.com/poison/mauna-loa-peace-lily/|title=Peace Lily |website=Pet Poison Helpline}}</ref>

== Diseases ==
Infection of peace lilies with ''[[Botrytis cinerea]]'' was first documented in [[Tokyo]], Japan from 1989 to 1994. [[Myrothecium roridum]] has also been used to harden ''in vitro'' cultures of the plant. ''[[Alternaria alternata]]'' leaf rot was documented on peace lilies in Argentina in 2008.<ref name="Saha2017">Mounika, K., Panja, B., & Saha, J. (2017). Diseases of peace lily [spathiphyllum sp.] caused by fungi, bacteria and viruses: A review. [https://www.thepharmajournal.com/archives/2017/vol6issue9/PartB/6-9-21-558.pdf]</ref>

== History ==
[[Heinrich Wilhelm Schott]] formally described the genus ''Spathiphyllum'' – literally "leaf spathe" – in his and [[Stephan Endlicher]]'s 1832 book ''Meletemata Botanica''. It encompassed two species: ''[[Spathiphyllum lanceifolium|S. lanceifolium]]'' (previously described as ''Dracontium lanceaefolium'' by [[Nikolaus Joseph von Jacquin]] in 1790) and ''S. sagittaefolium''.<ref name=Bunting1960/> Examinations of similar specimens by others resulted in new genera: [[Frederik Liebmann]]'s ''Hydnostachyon'' in 1849 and [[Karl Koch (botanist)|Karl Koch]]'s ''Massowia'' in 1852. Schott redefined ''Spathiphyllum'' in 1853, moving ''S. sagittaefolium'' into the new genus ''[[Urospatha]]'', and claiming ''Massowia'' and ''Hydnostachyon'' to be more appropriately ''Spathiphyllum''.<ref name=Bunting1960/> Just five years later, Schott's ''Prodromus Systematis Aroidearum'' expanded ''Spathiphyllum'' to 22 species.<ref name=Bunting1960/> From there, the genus remained relatively stable. Collections that included [[type specimen]]s of many ''Spathiphyllum'' were destroyed by fire in Vienna (1945, where Schott had worked) and by war in Berlin (where [[Adolf Engler]] had described several ''Spathiphyllum'' species).<ref name=Bunting1960/> [[George S. Bunting]] revised the genus as his PhD thesis work in 1960, encompassing a total 36 species.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://plants.jstor.org/stable/10.5555/al.ap.person.bm000001169 |accessdate=4 April 2024 |title=Bunting, George Sydney (1927-2015) |publisher=JSTOR - Global Plants}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=A Review of Studies of Neotropical Araceae |author=Croat TB |date=2015 |volume=38 |issue=1 |journal=Aroideana |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/Portals/0/staff/PDFs/croat/AReviewOfStudiesOfNeotropical%20Araceae.pdf |accessdate=4 April 2024 |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden}}</ref>
